item.title: Doctors report less burnout in practices they rate as efficient, even during long workweeks
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear reporting on physician burnout and efficiency

Doctors report less burnout in practices they rate as efficient, even during long workweeks

When it comes to physician burnout, how you spend your working hours may matter more than how many hours you work.

A new study led by Stanford Medicine researchers, published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, found that physicians who perceived their clinical practices as more efficient reported less burnout, greater professional fulfillment and less intention to leave their jobs, regardless of how many hours they worked each week.

The findings suggest that improving clinical workflows, reducing administrative burdens and making better use of care teams could be important strategies for addressing physician burnout.

"This is good news if you're a clinician or a health system administrator and you're worried about productivity, but you're also worried about physician well-being," said Bryan Bohman, M.D., associate chief medical officer for Stanford Medicine's Workforce Health and Wellness and the lead author of the study.

"You may not need to 'balance' those two goals, one against the other; in fact, our data suggest that you may be able to improve both well-being and productivity by focusing on improving practice efficiency."

Not just about hours worked

The researchers analyzed survey responses from 16,649 physicians at 14 academic health systems across the United States. The survey asked them about their experiences with clinical workflows, scheduling, administrative responsibilities and other factors that could affect their ability to provide care efficiently.

Physicians who rated their practices as more efficient reported significantly less burnout and greater professional fulfillment. Physicians who perceived their practices as more efficient were also substantially less likely to report an intent to leave their employer within two years.

The relationship between efficiency and burnout remained strong even after researchers accounted for hours worked. In fact, physicians who reported low practice efficiency and worked 40 hours or fewer per week experienced more burnout than those who reported high efficiency and worked 66 hours or more.

"What we doctors want is to give high-quality care to our patients in an efficient way," said Bohman, a clinical professor of primary care and population health. "That makes us feel fulfilled, and it reduces burnout—even when we work long hours."

That doesn't mean long work hours are harmless. Previous research has consistently linked excessive work hours with physician burnout, and this study didn't establish that inefficiency causes burnout. But the findings suggest that reducing work hours isn't the only way—and alone may not be enough—to improve physicians' experience.

Inefficiency impedes good patient care

Efficiency isn't simply about how many patients a physician sees or how quickly they complete their work. It's also about whether the systems around them make it easier or harder to provide high-quality care.

Consider a surgeon whose first surgery starts late because the operating room isn't ready. Or a doctor who must track down missing imaging results, take on tasks that could be handled by other care team members or finish documentation after an already full day of appointments.

Together these problems can make the workday frustrating, unpredictable and unnecessarily demanding. They can also have an impact on personal life, further exacerbating burnout and reducing the quality of care.

"In other research, we've shown that the impact of work on personal relationships has a very high correlation with burnout—they didn't make it to the wedding, the violin recital, the soccer game because it took an hour and a half to prepare the operating room for the final surgery of the day," Bohman said.

To capture physicians' workplace experiences, the researchers asked physicians whether operational problems interfere with patient care, make it difficult to stay on schedule or prevent them from completing their work during the day. Other questions addressed the availability of patient information, appropriate delegation of tasks and whether the clinical environment feels chaotic or unpredictable.

Finding the friction points

The researchers say the questions on their survey could help health system leaders identify where operational problems may be contributing to burnout.

If physicians at one outpatient clinic, for example, report substantially lower efficiency than those at another location, administrators may be able to pinpoint the problem, with the understanding that it could be contributing to burnout and professional dissatisfaction. Bohman recommends bringing physicians together with operational and quality improvement leaders to develop solutions.

There are still unanswered questions. The study relied on physicians' perceptions rather than objective measures of efficiency or productivity. Because it captured responses at a single point in time, it also cannot determine whether improving efficiency would directly reduce burnout. Future research could examine how perceived efficiency relates to quantifiable productivity and whether changes in efficiency lead to improvements in physician well-being.

"A productive clinical day where we provide good-quality care to more patients is an important element of our professional fulfillment and helps protect us against burnout," Bohman said.

Researchers from Texas A&M University, College of Medicine; the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health; The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center; and Yale University School of Medicine contributed to the study.

Publication details

Bryan Bohman et al., Associations of Perceived Efficiency of Clinical Practice With Physician Well-Being, Mayo Clinic Proceedings (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.mayocp.2026.08.018

Journal information: Mayo Clinic Proceedings

item.title: Novel metric accurately distinguishes metastasis from an independent primary tumor
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original research on tumor differentiation

Novel metric accurately distinguishes metastasis from an independent primary tumor

Research has found that the newly developed Clonal Relatedness Index (CRI) can accurately determine whether tumors in the same patient share a common clonal origin. The findings, detailed in an article appearing in The Journal of Molecular Diagnostics, have important implications for the clinical management of complex cases of cancers of the digestive system and abdominal lining, specifically gastrointestinal, hepatopancreatobiliary and peritoneal carcinomas.

"When two tumors arise in the same patient, one of the most crucial questions is whether they are related or represent independent primaries," explains lead author Namrata Setia, M.D., Department of Anatomic Pathology, University of Chicago. "This is particularly challenging when tumors in different organs share overlapping cellular features, or when genomic complexity limits the diagnostic clarity of conventional markers. Even experienced pathologists can reach the limits of microscopic and marker-based evaluation."

The researchers of this study analyzed 60 pairs of gastrointestinal, hepatopancreatobiliary and peritoneal tumors using targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) data and developed the CRI, which is calculated as the number of shared genomic alterations divided by the average number of alterations in the two tumors. CRI outperformed conventional phenotype-based assessment in distinguishing whether a tumor has metastasized or whether it represents a new independent lesion.

First author Gertruda Evaristo, M.D., Department of Anatomic Pathology, University of Chicago, and Department of Pathology, McGill University, adds, "Unlike more complex statistical approaches that require specialized software or biostatistical expertise, we aimed to turn genomic data that laboratories already generate into a simple, quantitative measure of tumor relatedness. The CRI does exactly that: it takes a complex diagnostic question and makes it more measurable, interpretable and potentially accessible to routine molecular pathology practice."

The CRI showed particular value in diagnostically challenging cases involving hypermutability, where morphologic and immunophenotypic overlap or divergence can complicate assessments of tumor relatedness. The method held up in a validation cohort, although it failed for one ultramutated POLE-mutated pair. The researchers urge particular caution in cases with extremely high mutational burden.

Potential clinical implications of using CRI are as follows:

- Diagnosis: The CRI may be particularly useful in cases with overlapping histologic features, limited tissue or unusual growth patterns that obscure tumor origin. It may also be valuable in patients with hereditary cancer syndromes or mismatch repair deficiency, in whom phenotype-based assessment can be unreliable.

- Prognosis: Misclassification can substantially alter the perceived extent of disease and expectations regarding clinical course. Although the investigators did not directly evaluate clinical outcomes, more accurate classification of metastatic disease versus independent primary tumors could improve staging and prognostic assessment.

- Treatment: More accurate classification could help avoid inappropriate systemic treatment for an independent primary or inadequate local treatment for metastatic disease. The extent to which CRI-guided classification changes clinical management or improves patient outcomes remains to be established.

"Although further validation is needed, especially across tumor types and sequencing platforms, our approach provides an accessible quantitative adjunct when conventional pathology reaches its limits," concludes Setia. "Sequencing is often used to identify actionable alterations, but the same data can tell us something fundamental about the relationship between tumors. We see an opportunity to extract more diagnostic value from genomic information that is already available."

Publication details

Gertruda Evaristo et al., Clonal Relatedness Index, The Journal of Molecular Diagnostics (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.jmoldx.2026.09.001

Journal information: Journal of Molecular Diagnostics

item.title: Low vitamin D could be keeping you up at night
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful information on vitamin D and sleep

Low vitamin D could be keeping you up at night

Tossing and turning at night? The problem might not be your mattress—it could be your vitamin D levels.

A new study suggests people with higher vitamin D levels may get more sleep and stay awake for shorter stretches during the night.

Researchers analyzed blood tests and sleep data from 460 middle-aged and older adults.

Those with the highest vitamin D levels slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night than those with the lowest levels, they found. And participants classified as vitamin D deficient averaged about 23 minutes less sleep than those with normal levels.

"These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health," said senior author Adam Spira, a sleep researcher at Johns Hopkins University.

The connection between vitamin D and sleep appeared stronger among Black participants.

But researchers noted that the study can't prove that low vitamin D causes poor sleep—or that taking supplements will improve it.

They also couldn't tell whether participants got their vitamin D from food, sunlight or supplements.

Future studies may examine whether the connection to better sleep differs depending on the vitamin's source.

The paper is published in The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences.

More information

Diefei Chen et al., Association of vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep in cognitively unimpaired middle-aged and older adults, The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences (2026). DOI: 10.1093/gerona/glag212

item.title: Mpox cases are on the rise again in Brazil – just as an antiviral drug fails in trials
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: report on mpox cases and antiviral drug trials

The city of Rio de Janeiro has reported 180 confirmed cases of mpox, an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus, MPXV, from Oct. 1 through Nov. 24, 2026.

Skin lesions are the most common sign of the disease. They can also appear in the mouth, on the genitals or in the anal region. Other symptoms include fever, swollen glands, headache, body aches, chills and weakness.

The number of cases in the capital of Rio de Janeiro is more than 22 times higher than the number reported during the same period in 2025. In the state of São Paulo, 128 cases have been identified from Oct.1 through Nov. 17, which represents almost half of all cases of the disease that the state has reported this year.

The national figures are not alarming: 1,429 confirmed cases and one death as of Nov. 23, compared to about 10,500 cases and 14 deaths in 2022.

The average, however, hides what really matters: The curve began to rise again in September, concentrated in two state capitals, with a new strain of the virus circulating that is different from the one identified in the previous outbreak.

In virology, a clade is a group of viral lineages that share a common ancestor. Currently, clade Ib predominates among the samples analyzed. The 2022 mpox outbreak was caused by clade IIb.

In response, the Ministry of Health purchased 25,000 doses of the vaccine against the disease and instructed states and municipalities to administer it intradermally – that is, just into the top layer of skin. This technique can increase the number of people vaccinated with the same vial fivefold.

The vaccine has become even more important in the fight against mpox, because the only antiviral drug available to treat the disease has just failed two clinical trials.

What has changed about the virus?

Clade Ib was identified in 2023 in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and led the World Health Organization to declare an international public health emergency in August 2024.

Following a sustained decline in reported cases in Central and East Africa, the WHO declared the end of this international public health emergency. It was then that prevention, surveillance and control of the disease became part of long-term public health programs.

At the Fiocruz National Institute of Infectious Diseases, or INI/Fiocruz, a leading center for the disease in Rio, 43 of the 62 samples identified between September and October 2026 were from clade Ib. Of the total, only 19 were from clade IIb.

Clade Ib was first detected in Rio in March 2026. The spike in diagnoses did not occur until September. In October, the institute treated 130 people with suspected cases of the disease and confirmed 89 cases.

Clade Ib arrived in Brazil via travelers. INI/Fiocruz identified the first cases with evidence of community transmission – people infected locally, with no recent travel history – in early 2026.

The question is whether clade Ib would cause more severe illness. In Central Africa, it has been associated with a higher case fatality rate than that observed with clade IIb, but this difference is also linked to factors such as malnutrition, co-infections and lack of access to care.

In Rio, INI/Fiocruz has not yet found any clinically significant difference between the two clades in the group of patients being monitored, which they call the Rio cohort. The profile of the most vulnerable individuals remains the same – those with severe immunosuppression, pregnant women and young children. About 45% of the patients in the Rio cohort are living with HIV.

Antiviral drug failed the test

During the 2022 outbreak, the antiviral drug tecovirimat was distributed as a treatment for mpox. The drug had been approved in the U.S. for smallpox based on animal studies, since there was no way to test it on people, as smallpox had been eradicated from the planet since 1980. But the emergence of mpox has made it possible to approve the drug for people.

An April 2025 trial compared the drug tecovirimat with a placebo in 597 patients with clade I in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The time to lesions clearing up was seven days in the group that received tecovirimat and eight days in the placebo group. This difference is not considered statistically significant.

In February 2026, a second trial settled the question regarding clade II. The study followed more than 400 adults divided into two groups, one that received the antiviral and another that received a placebo. Through Day 29, the estimated rates of lesion resolution were similar in the two groups – 83% with tecovirimat and 84% with the placebo. The study found no evidence that tecovirimat was able to accelerate lesion resolution in adults with clade II mpox.

Thus, mpox remains a disease without a proven specific treatment, which shifts the focus of the response to early diagnosis, isolation and vaccination. The medication remains reserved for patients with severe cases and immunosuppressed patients, even though there is no evidence that it alters the course of the disease in these patients.

What the vaccine does

The only vaccine for mpox is MVA-BN, also known as Jynneos, a third-generation, nonreplicating smallpox vaccine produced by Bavarian Nordic in Denmark. It has not been tested in randomized trials to assess its efficacy against mpox. There are, however, observational studies conducted in the context of the 2022 outbreak, all involving clade IIb. In these studies, researchers do not determine who receives the vaccine, but simply monitor patient outcomes.

Based on these observational studies, the WHO estimates that this vaccine reduces the risk of mpox by 76% with one dose and by 82% with two, compared to unvaccinated individuals. Results varied from one study to another, particularly with a single dose. Estimates of risk reduction ranged from 35% to 86% with one dose and from 66% to 90% with two doses.…

Source: The Conversation Health | Published: 2026-11-24 21:09 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Weak and immature management putting patients at risk at failing health board, review finds
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: report on health board management issues

Weak and immature management putting patients at risk at failing health board, review finds

Wales' largest health board is still failing, with "fundamental weaknesses" in governance and management, a new report says.

Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board has been in special measures for nine years in total, with the latest period starting in 2023.

A review of its leadership published on Tuesday found, in some parts, targets and money "have a greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care".

Committed staff and ability to deliver some strong local services were highlighted.

The health board apologised and said it now needed to concentrate on improving its leadership and allowing its staff to "flourish".

The review was commissioned by the Welsh government in the summer, after it gave Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board (BCUHB) a "final chance" to improve.

It concluded that senior leadership was "immature and ineffective", with weak senior management putting the quality of patient care at risk.

The review did not suggest splitting up the health board, but Wales' health minister said the findings were "unacceptable" and BCUHB "does not function as a single coherent organisation".

The report said: "Many areas reported a culture where targets and financial matters have a greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care.

"Fear of speaking up was described often... staff did not believe that raising a concern would result in corrective action.

"Despite this, the panel witnessed many teams striving to deliver the very best care they could for patients."

The reviewers also found a "toxic" culture at the health board where staff were afraid to speak out, and worried that no-one would listen if they did.

The chair of BCUHB, Dyfed Edwards apologised for the health board's failings.

"We haven't done things as we should," he said. "We have got things wrong.

"We need to take a step back from all the firefighting that has been going on, and address key things.

"We need to allow staff to show leadership and to flourish, and for us all to get systems in place which will allow us to address key performance issues like waiting times."

The health board's chief executive, Carol Shillabeer, previously announced she would be leaving in the new year to take up an NHS role in England.

Her departure follows a string of other senior leaders who have left the organisation in recent months, including the chief operating officer and executive director of finance.

The report also said that bureaucracy and slow decision-making led to a "loss of local ownership" and staff feeling frustrated.

'Betsi spaghetti'

The reviewers wrote: "Staff and leaders described decisions moving through multiple layers of approval, authority becoming concentrated at senior levels and operational leaders lacking sufficient autonomy to act.

"A phrase used in a focus group characterised the resulting complexity as 'Betsi spaghetti'."

However, the review concluded the health board could still be improved without being broken up into smaller organisations - an option previously discussed by ministers.

It said staff were "loyal and committed", and there were "strong local services" and "significant clinical expertise across north Wales".

Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor said: "these failings are utterly unacceptable".

"I also share the understandable frustrations of staff and patients alike in north Wales at the lack of progress in delivering and embedding improvements to services and standards of care," he said.

"The report identifies that the health board does not currently demonstrate the organisational conditions required to deliver and sustain reliable improvement."

But the health minister rejected calls for radical action or structural change to the NHS in north Wales.

He said he would be making an order to appoint a new deputy chief executive and an independent board governance advisor. The post of vice chair - currently vacant - would also be filled.

Professor Medwin Hughes, chair of the patients' watchdog Llais said: "There should be no more final chances â significant concerns have been expressed over many years by patients, and now is the time to really address these.

"It's not good enough just to identify the issues. We now need there to be realistic targets and outcomes that deliver for patients and that deliver for citizens."

'People are dying'

Benjamin Hodge Mckenna MS, Reform UK Wales's health spokesperson, said BCUHB had been "plagued by mismanagement, poor performance and repeated failures".

"Senior leaders and government ministers cannot continue to preside over failure without facing consequences," he said.

Darren Millar MS, leader of the Welsh Conservatives, said: "These damning findings are sadly nothing new.

"Putting the health board in special measures was supposed to improve performance, yet things have got worse and people are dying as a result."

Ken Skates, Welsh Labour spokesperson for health, said the people of north Wales "deserve clear evidence that sustained improvement will be delivered".

"Progress and accountability were disappointingly absent from today's announcement," he said.

item.title: GP surgery suspends routine appointments due to 'tsunami' of demand
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: report on GP surgery appointment suspension

GP surgery suspends routine appointments due to 'tsunami' of demand

A GP surgery has suspended all routine appointments due to what it calls a "tsunami" of demand.

It is the second time in a week that Aberfoyle Medical Practice in Londonderry has told patients that it is not offering routine appointments - either in person or online.

Dr Donna Mace, who is a partner at the practice and also a member of the Northern Ireland General Practitioners' Committee, said the practice was currently dealing with unprecedented demand.

In real terms, that means their doctors are seeing around 60 patients a day, which she said was not safe.

The Department of Health (DoH) said general practices across Northern Ireland "continue to experience significant demand for services".

At times, the department said, practices may need to "to implement temporary measures to manage patient care safely and effectively".

As independent contractors GP surgeries are responsible for managing their own appointment systems, DoH said.

Prioritising of urgent appointments according to clinical need, the department added, is an "established approach within health care."

"Aberfoyle is one of the biggest practices in Derry and we are really fortunate in that we have 11 doctors, social workers, physios, mental health practitioners and counsellors but unfortunately the last few weeks have just not been manageable at all," Dr Mace told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.

"Every single day the appointments have been filled up, so much so, that every on-call doctor is dealing with 60 patients per day.

"In my on-call, that is dealing with emergency mental health patients, patients in palliative care and very ill children and it was just not manageable," she said.

"I am a partner at the practice and we employ four salaried doctors and there was a risk of losing those doctors If we lost them due to stress or resignation because they couldn't cope, that would mean we would lose 100 appointments so we had to manage the risk.

"They couldn't go on and there was a total crisis."

The doctor said the decision was taken due to concerns about patient safety.

"It was not manageable and it was not safe, no patient is going to appreciate if we miss something because we have less than the usual 10 minutes with them," she said.

The doctor said they could only deal with urgent appointments and apologised to all those affected.

In October, the practice saw more then 4,000 patients face-to-face, handled 1,500 telephone consultations and dealt with nearly 9,000 prescription issues.

The practice would review the situation on a "day-to-day basis" to determine when it could reopen routine appointments.

item.title: How antibody therapy reverses type 1 diabetes in mice
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: explanation of antibody therapy for type 1 diabetes

How antibody therapy reverses type 1 diabetes in mice

Researchers at UC Davis Health have uncovered key mechanisms behind an experimental antibody that reverses type 1 diabetes (T1D) in mice. Findings from their study, published in the journal Diabetes, could advance efforts to develop treatments for patients with acute T1D.

Previous studies have shown that T1D can be prevented in mice. However, preventing the condition has limited clinical relevance because most patients are diagnosed only after they have developed the disease and require treatment.

T1D occurs when the body's immune system mistakenly attacks insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. As these cells are destroyed, the body loses its ability to regulate blood sugar levels, requiring lifelong insulin therapy.

Current treatments manage the disease but do not reverse the underlying autoimmune process.

"Most people are diagnosed with T1D after the disease has already developed and significant damage has occurred to the insulin-producing cells," said William Ridgway, chief of rheumatology, allergy & clinical immunology at UC Davis Health. "To help patients, we need therapies that can reverse the disease process. Our study helps explain how this experimental treatment works and identifies biological pathways that could one day be targeted in people with T1D."

A new approach to type 1 diabetes

Most experimental treatments for T1D focus on T cells, components of the adaptive immune system that attack insulin-producing beta cells. Ridgway and his colleagues instead investigated the role of the innate immune system, a less-studied branch of immune biology in type 1 diabetes.

The team utilized a mouse model of T1D and advanced single-cell sequencing to show that antibody treatment produced myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). MDSCs are specialized immune cells that help control inflammation. The antibody treatment induced the MDSCs to travel to the pancreatic islet and reduced the immune activity responsible for damaging beta cells.

The team also found that the treatment depended on the anti-inflammatory signaling molecule interleukin-10 (IL-10). Without IL-10, MDSCs failed to develop, and the therapy lost its ability to reverse diabetes.

"These findings show that innate immune cells may play a much larger role in controlling autoimmune diabetes than previously appreciated," Ridgway said.

Reduction in beta-cell stress

One of the study's most significant discoveries involved beta cells.

As T1D progresses, surviving beta cells experience increasing stress. Not only are they under attack from the immune system, but they must also work harder to produce enough insulin to meet the body's needs. Over time, this stress can contribute to beta-cell dysfunction and death.

The researchers found that shortly after treatment, biological markers of cellular stress within beta cells dropped dramatically. Specifically, the therapy reduced pathways associated with endoplasmic reticulum stress and the unfolded protein response—both of which are linked to beta-cell damage.

"One of the findings we were most excited about was the profound reduction in beta-cell stress," Ridgway said. "As far as we know, this is the first study to closely examine what happens inside the pancreas after T1D has been reversed."

Ridgway and his fellow researchers believe lowering stress on the remaining insulin-producing cells may be an important factor in restoring normal blood sugar levels and preserving beta-cell function.

Potential impact beyond type 1 diabetes

While the findings are limited to mouse models and additional research is needed before human studies can begin, the investigators believe the work could have implications beyond T1D.

"Understanding how these specialized immune cells develop and function may help us identify new treatment strategies not only for T1D, but potentially for other autoimmune diseases as well," Ridgway said.

Future studies will focus on adapting the approach for human therapeutics and determining whether similar mechanisms can be safely activated in patients.

Nicolle K. Martin et al., Reversal of T1D and Rapid Reduction of β-Cell Stress by IL-10–Dependent MDSCs Induced by TLR4-Ab, Diabetes (2026). DOI: 10.2337/db26-0636
